'''''Albizia julibrissin''''', the '''Persian silk tree''', '''pink silk tree''', or '''mimosa tree''', is a [[species]] of tree in the [[Fabaceae]] family, native to [[Western Asia|southwestern]] and [[East Asia|eastern]] Asia.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://gardens.co.nz/PlantoftheWeek.cfm?NLID=96 |title=Plant of the Week |publisher=Gardens.co.nz |access-date=2014-04-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130208135835/http://gardens.co.nz/PlantoftheWeek.cfm?NLID=96 |archive-date=2013-02-08 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
It was introduced to Europe in the mid-18th century by Italian nobleman Filippo degli [[Albizzi]], and the name of its entire genus [[Albizzia|Albizia]] is given after him.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/albizia-julibrissin/ |title=Albizia julibrissin (Mimosa, Persian Silk Tree, Pink Silk Tree, Silk Tree)  |website= North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|access-date=17 February 2021 }}</ref> The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''julibrissin'' is a corruption of the [[Persian language|Persian]] word {{Transliteration|fa|gul-i abrisham}} ({{lang|fa|گل ابریشم}}), which means "[[silk flower]]" (from {{Transliteration|fa|gul}} {{lang|fa|گل}} "flower" + {{Transliteration|fa|abrisham}} {{lang|fa|ابریشم}} "[[silk]]").<ref name=":1" />{{additional citation needed |date=June 2024 |reason=Other offline jrnls with Persian nm, only source available online “FORESTS AND FORESTRY i. In Persia,” in Encyclopædia Iranica mentioning "abrīšam"}}

''Albizia julibrissin'' was described by [[species:Antonio Durazzini|Antonio Durazzini]]. 

== Names ==
''Albizia julibrissin'' is known by a wide variety of common names, such as '''Persian silk tree''' and '''pink siris'''. It is also called '''[[Lankaran]] acacia''' or '''bastard tamarind''', though it is not too closely related to either genus. The species is called '''Chinese silk tree''', '''silk tree''' or '''mimosa''' in the United States, which is misleading—the former can refer to any species of ''[[Albizia]]'' which is most common in any one locale; and, although once included in ''[[Mimosa]]'', neither is it very close to the [[Mimoseae]]. To add to the confusion, several species of ''[[Acacia]]'', notably ''[[Acacia baileyana]]'' and ''[[Acacia dealbata]]'', are also known as "mimosa" (especially in [[floristry]]), and many [[Fabaceae]] trees with highly divided leaves are called thus in [[horticulture]].

[[File:Jungpflanze des Seidenbaums (Schlafbaum).png|thumb|Sleeping tree by day and night]]
Its leaves slowly close during the night and during periods of rain, the leaflets bowing downward; thus its modern Persian name '''{{Transliteration|fa|shabkhosb}}''' ({{lang|fa|شب‌خسب}}) means "night sleeper". This tendency also explains the Chinese common name '''hehuan''', which means "shut happy" and symbolizes a happy couple in bed.<ref name=":0" /> In Japan its common names are '''{{Transliteration|ja|nemunoki}}''', '''{{Transliteration|ja|nemurinoki}}''' and '''{{Transliteration|ja|nenenoki}}''' which all mean "sleeping tree". '''Nemu tree''' is a partial translation of {{Transliteration|ja|nemunoki}}.

== Description ==
[[File:Copper sunbird (Cinnyris cupreus cupreus) female on Persian silk tree (Albizia julibrissin).jpg|thumb|''[[Cinnyris cupreus]]'' and flower]]
[[File:Albizia julibrissin flower.jpg|alt=close up image of albizia julibrissin flower|thumb|''Albizia julibrissin'' flower]]
''Albizia julibrissin'' is a small [[deciduous]] tree with a broad crown of level or arching branches, growing to {{convert|5–16|m|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Klingaman |first=Gerald |date=July 23, 2004 |title=Mimosa |url=https://www.uaex.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/mimosa.aspx|url-status=live|access-date=February 16, 2021 |website=University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140329122542/http://www.uaex.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/mimosa.aspx |archive-date=March 29, 2014 }}</ref> Its [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is dark greenish grey, becoming vertically striped with age. Its [[leaf|leaves]] are large and [[frond]]-like: They are [[pinnate|bipinnate]], divided into 6–12 pairs of pinnae, each with 20–30 pairs of leaflets. Individual leaflets are oblong, {{convert|1–1.5|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2–4|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} broad. The true leaves are {{convert|20–45|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|12–25|cm|0|abbr=on}} broad.

[[File:A.jul-flor-9-en.jpg|thumb|Flowers, parts]]
[[File:Eurema blanda laying eggs by kadavoor.JPG|thumb|''[[Eurema blanda]]'' laying eggs on ''A. julibrissin'']]
The [[flower]]s bloom throughout the summer in dense [[inflorescence]]s, which resemble starbursts of pink silky threads. The true flowers have small [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] and [[petal|corolla]] (except the central ones), with a tight cluster of prominent [[stamen]]s, 2–3 cm long and white or pink with a white base. They have been observed to attract [[bee]]s, [[butterfly|butterflies]] and [[hummingbird]]s.<ref name=":1" /> Its [[fruit]] is a flat brown [[legume|pod]] {{convert|10–20|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2–2.5|cm|1|abbr=on}} broad, containing several [[seeds]] inside.

There are two [[variety (biology)|varieties]]:
* ''Albizia julibrissin'' var. ''julibrissin'' – the typical variety, described above
* ''Albizia julibrissin'' var. ''mollis'' – differs in the shoots being densely hairy

==Habitat, cultivation and uses==
Original habitats of the tree include regions from [[Iran]] (Persia) and the [[Republic of Azerbaijan]] to [[China]] and [[Korea]].<ref>Juan-Alberto Rodriguez Pérez, Flore exotique dans les îles Canaries, Leon, Espagne, Editorial Everest, 1990. {{ISBN|84-241-4668-9}}). Page 11</ref>

''A. julibrissin'' is widely planted as an [[ornamental plant]] in parks and gardens, grown for its fine leaf texture, flowers and attractive horizontal canopy. Other positive attributes are a fast growth rate, low water requirements and the ability to thrive planted in full sun in hot summer climates.<ref name="Kathleen Norris Brenzel ed. 2007 178">{{cite book| title=Sunset Western Garden Book | editor=Kathleen Norris Brenzel | year=2007 | page=178 }}</ref> It is frequently planted in semi-arid areas like California's [[Central Valley (California)|Central Valley]], central [[Texas]] and [[Oklahoma]]. Although capable of surviving drought, growth will be stunted and the tree tends to look sickly. As such it should be given infrequent, deep waterings during the summer, which will benefit growth and flowering.<ref name="Kathleen Norris Brenzel ed. 2007 178"/>

The broad crown of a mature tree makes it useful for providing dappled shade. The flower colour varies from white in ''A. julibrissin'' f. ''alba'', to rich red-tipped flowers. Variants with cream or pale yellow flowers are also reported. Other cultivars are becoming available: 'Summer Chocolate' has red foliage ageing to dark bronze, with pale pink flowers; 'Ishii Weeping' (or 'Pendula') has a drooping growth habit.

===''A. julibrissin'' f. ''rosea''===
There is also a [[Form (botany)|form]], ''A. julibrissin'' f. ''rosea'' (pink silk tree) which has, in the past, been classed either as a variety or as a [[cultivar]]. This is a smaller tree, only growing to {{convert|5–7|m|0}} tall, with the flowers always pink. Native to the northeast of the species' range in Korea and Northern China, it is more cold-tolerant than the typical form, surviving temperatures down to at least {{convert|-25|°C}}. The selected [[cultivar]] ''A. julibrissin'' 'Ernest Wilson' (also known as 'E.H.Wilson' or 'Rosea') is a cold-tolerant tree with deep pink flower colour. In Japan, ''A. julibrissin'' f. ''rosea'' is often used for non-traditional [[bonsai]]. The name {{Transliteration|ja|nemunoki*}} ({{lang|ja|ねむの木}}, [[Kanji]]: {{lang|ja-hani|合歓木}}) and its variants is a ''[[kigo]]'' representing the summer in [[haiku]], especially a sleepy summer evening.<ref name=kigo>{{cite web |url=http://kigosai.sub.jp/kigo500a/377.html |script-title=ja:合歓の花（ねむのはな） 晩夏 |publisher=kigosai.sub.jp |access-date=2011-06-27|language=ja}}</ref>

''A. julibrissin'' f. ''rosea'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]];<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/77621/Albizia-julibrissin-f-rosea/Details |title=RHS Plant Selector ''Albizia julibrissin'' f. ''rosea'' AGM / RHS Gardening |publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk |access-date=2020-03-12}}</ref> likewise the cultivar 'Summer Chocolate'.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/258154/Albizia-julibrissin-Summer-Chocolate-(PBR)/Details | title = ''Albizia julibrissin'' 'Summer Chocolate' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 27 February 2020}}</ref>

===Other uses===
Silk tree wood may be used to make furniture.<ref>{{Cite web|date=November 20, 2019|title=Albizia julibrissin (silk tree)|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/4005#touses|url-status=live|access-date=February 16, 2021|website=CABI Invasive Species Compendium|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170723181538/http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/4005 |archive-date=2017-07-23 }}</ref> It is also reportedly psychoactive as well, with the flowers being used to make teas. In Chinese medicine it is considered an antidepressant.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Huang | first1=Bishan | last2=Wu | first2=Yingyao | last3=Li | first3=Chan | last4=Tang | first4=Qingfa | last5=Zhang | first5=Yuanwei | title=Molecular basis and mechanism of action of Albizia julibrissin in depression treatment and clinical application of its formulae | journal=Chinese Herbal Medicines | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=15 | issue=2 | year=2023 | issn=1674-6384 | doi=10.1016/j.chmed.2022.10.004 | pages=201–213| pmid=37265761 | pmc=10230641 }}</ref>

==Invasive species==
[[File:Silktreemap.PNG|left|thumb|Distribution of ''A. julibrissin'' in the United States]]
[[File:Albizia julibrissin 399607729.jpg|thumb|''A. julibrissin'' in Cape May, New Jersey]]
In the wild, the tree tends to grow in dry plains, sandy valleys, and uplands. It has become an [[invasive species]] in the [[United States]], where it has spread from southern New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, west to Missouri and Illinois, and south to Florida and Texas. It is cultivated in California and Oregon.{{citation needed|date=March 2014}} Its seeds are wind-dispersed and numerous, and they are fertile even over long periods of drought. Each pod, which resembles a flattened bean pod made of paper, holds about 8 seeds on average. The pod bursts in strong winds, and the seeds can carry over long distances.

Breeding work is currently underway in the United States to produce ornamental plants which will not set seed and can be planted without risk of invasive spread.{{citation needed|date=December 2020}} However, in the eastern United States it is generally a short-lived tree, being highly susceptible to mimosa vascular wilt,<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20120302043734/http://www.pubs.ext.vt.edu/2811/2811-1020/2811-1020.html Fusarium Wilt of Mimosa (''Albizia julibrissin'')], Virginia Cooperative Extension</ref> a fungal disease caused by a species of ''[[Fusarium]]'', though the disease does not seem to have seriously impacted its populations. Because of its invasive tendencies and disease susceptibility, it is rarely recommended as an ornamental plant in the United States, though it is still widely planted in parts of Europe.
